module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Pierpont primes

A Pierpont prime is a prime of the form $2^a 3^b + 1$, where $a$ and $b$ are
nonnegative integers. Marc Gleason conjectured that there are infinitely many.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Pierpont prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierpont_prime)
- [OEIS A005109](https://oeis.org/A005109)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace PierpontPrime

/-- A Pierpont prime is a prime of the form $2^a3^b + 1$. -/
def IsPierpontPrime (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p.Prime ∧ ∃ a b : ℕ, p = 2 ^ a * 3 ^ b + 1

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem two_isPierpontPrime : IsPierpontPrime 2 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 0, 0, ?_⟩
  norm_num

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem thirtySeven_isPierpontPrime : IsPierpontPrime 37 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 2, 2, ?_⟩
  norm_num

/-- There are infinitely many Pierpont primes. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinitely_many_pierpont_primes :
    Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | IsPierpontPrime p} := by
  sorry

end PierpontPrime

findings.description: The module docstring at line 24 attributes the infinitude conjecture to “Marc Gleason”. Both cited sources identify Andrew M. Gleason. This is a reference-attribution slip; the Lean mathematics is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia’s “Distribution” section states: “Andrew M. Gleason made this reasoning explicit, conjecturing there are infinitely many Pierpont primes” (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierpont_prime). OEIS A005109 also credits Andrew M. Gleason in its reference to “Angle Trisection, the Heptagon and the Triskaidecagon”, read via https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A005/A005109.seq.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace “Marc Gleason” with “Andrew M. Gleason” in the module docstring.

review.notes: All four declarations faithfully state the cited mathematics. Wikipedia still records infinitude as unproved, consistent with `research open`. Lean experiments in /workspace/review/scratch.lean verified boundary cases, proved a decidable bounded-exponent characterization, reproduced the source’s sequence through 200, and checked that the infinitude statement is equivalent to unboundedly many prime values. Both existing test proofs are sorry-free. OEIS’s main site returned an access challenge, so its entry was read through the official OEIS data mirror.
